recall that a positive integer n and two integers a, b, gcd (a, n) = gcd (b, n) if and only if a and b generate the same ideal in the ring Z. / n. This is also equivalent to the condition that a = ub (mod n) for some u € (Z / n) . This property generalizes well for Artinian rings, and in particular, to finite rings. More precisely

Lemma 2.2. (See [5, Lemma 2.1] Let R be an Artinian ring. If Ra = Rb, then there exists u E R× such that b = ua.

From this perspective, a crucial observation here is that a generating set S in a finite ring R such as Z / n or Fqx] / f gives rise to a gcd-graph it and only if S is stable under the action of R; that is, if s € S, then us € S for all u € R*. Motivated by this observation, we introduce the following definition.

Definition 2.3. We say that I (R, S) is a gcd-graph if S is stable under the action of R.

Remark 2.4. When S = R*, the graph I (R, R*) is known as a unitary Cayley graph (see 11, 61). This shows that the unitary Cayley graph over R is a special case of gcd-graphs. Other examples, as explained previously, include the ged-graphs defined in [6] for the ring Z /n and the gcd-graphs defined in [9] for the ring Fq x|/ f where Fq is a finite field with q elements and f is a non-zero polynomial in IF q [x].

We provide below the necessary and sufficient conditions for a Cayley graph over R to be a gcd-graph. These conditions are somewhat more explicit than Definition 2.3. Furthermore, together with Corollary 2.7, this description will be important later on when we study the spectrum of these ged-graphs.

Proposition 2.5. Let R be a finite commutative ring and S a subset of R. Then the following are equivalent. (1) I(R,S) is a ged-graph. (2) There exist distinct nonzero principal ideals 11,12, ...,Ik such that for each r € R, r E S if and only if there exists 1 ≤ i ≤ k such that I; = Rr.

Proof. First, we claim that (2) → (1). Clearly, S is symmetric and 0 & S. By definition, we need to show that if s € S and u € R then us € S. Since s € S, there exists an ideal I; with 1 ≤ i ≤ k such that Rs = Ik. Since u € R, Ik = Rs = Rus. By (2), this shows that us € S. Let us show that (1) implies (2) as well. For each s € S, Let Is = Rs be the ideal generated by s. Let {I1, 12,..., Ik; be the set of all Is. We conclude that for each s € S, Is = I; for some 1 ≤ i ≤ k. Conversely, if r € R such that Rr € {11,1½,..., Ik›, then Rr = Rs for some s € S. By Lemma 2.2, we know that r = us for some u € R×. Since I (R, S) is a ged-graph, S is stable under the action of R×. This shows that r € S as well.
